evaluation.positioning_hook: A restless queer teen follows her childhood best friend into the woods to prove unicorns are real, only to discover the magic is tied to the identity she’s been trying not to name.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional promise is clear and accessible — first love, identity, and a magical reveal — but the film plays very intimate and artful rather than broad. The audience is real, especially for elevated coming-of-age and queer fantasy buyers, but this is not built as a four-quadrant commercial play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early and cleanly: a boy who saw a unicorn as a child drags his best friend on a search that turns into a discovery about her own nature. The birthday opening, the gas-station debate, and the woods search all keep the premise legible and escalating.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Alma and David are distinct and playable: he’s earnest, obsessive, and emotionally transparent; she’s guarded, funny, and increasingly conflicted. Their dynamic has real charm, though the script is more mood-and-identity driven than built around a deeply layered ensemble.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s boldness is in treating unicorn mythology as a queer coming-of-age metaphor without flattening it into allegory. The sound design, time-shifted transitions, and the final grotesque-beautiful horn reveal give it a confident, ownable artistic identity.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The search structure gives the film forward motion, but much of the middle is built on atmosphere, repeated conversation, and emotional circling. The final stretch pays off the tension, yet the engine is more cumulative than propulsive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: This is a fresh fusion of teen friendship, queer self-recognition, and magical realism that feels specific rather than generic. The unicorn reveal is surprising but emotionally inevitable because the script seeds Alma’s discomfort, the church imagery, and the repeated shimmer motif from the start.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world is specific in texture — bilingual family life, church culture, gas-station hangouts, bedroom details, and the visual grammar around shimmer and sound. It’s evocative, but the world functions more as a lived-in container for the central relationship than as a fully generative system.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually distinct: tender, dreamy, and slightly uncanny, with moments of grounded teen friction and a final burst of body-horror beauty. The repeated silence/sound shifts and the lyrical camera language make it hard to mistake for anything else.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The script suggests more beneath the surface through Alma’s family tension, the church sermon about being different, and the final bodily transformation. It’s not opaque, but it does imply a deeper internal mythology around identity, faith, and self-acceptance.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Alma-David bond carries the film and has enough friction to sustain the runtime, while the parents and clerk add texture. Still, this is fundamentally a two-person engine rather than a relationship web that generates many combinations.

lead_characters.name: Alma
lead_characters.hook: A guarded, observant queer teen who has outgrown the childhood magic she used to share with David, Alma is caught between wanting to dismiss the unicorn hunt and being terrified that it might explain who she really is. She reads as cool and resistant on the surface, but the script keeps exposing the tenderness, shame, and awe underneath, especially in the gas-station scene, the family confrontation, and the final mirror sequence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Rachel Zegler in West Side Story — a young woman carrying longing, defiance, and vulnerability in the same frame, with a final transformation that asks for emotional precision and physical metaphor at once.

lead_characters.name: David
lead_characters.hook: David is the believer: earnest, stubborn, a little theatrical, and emotionally naked in a way that keeps the story moving. He’s not just chasing a unicorn; he’s chasing proof that wonder survives adulthood, and his need to be right is really a need not to be alone in what he saw.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Lucas Hedges in Manchester by the Sea and Justice Smith in The Get Down their best material — a sensitive, impulsive young man whose sincerity becomes the engine of the scene and the emotional counterweight to the lead.

lead_characters.name: Alma's Mom
lead_characters.hook: Warm, practical, and emotionally direct, Alma’s mother is the family voice that keeps trying to pull Alma back into the room. Her bilingual dialogue and final hug give the film its clearest expression of love without full understanding.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded parent role that lets an actor play authority, tenderness, and cultural specificity in the same scene — the sort of showcase seen in Adriana Barraza’s work in Babel.

lead_characters.name: David's Mom
lead_characters.hook: David’s mother is the other half of the film’s domestic world: blunt, affectionate, and unbothered by the kids’ weirdness. She gives the story a lived-in neighborhood texture and reinforces that David’s wonder is happening inside a real family, not a fantasy vacuum.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a compact but flavorful mother role in the vein of Patricia Clarkson in Pieces of April — a scene-stealing adult presence that can make a small amount of screen time feel memorable.

lead_characters.name: Clerk
lead_characters.demographics: Young woman, late teens to early 20s
lead_characters.hook: The gas-station clerk is a quiet catalyst: cool, observant, and just ambiguous enough to trigger Alma’s attention and the film’s first real shimmer of possibility. She’s less a plot driver than a charged presence who makes the world feel awake.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of brief but magnetic role that can become a calling card if played with stillness and subtext — the sort of part that gave Jena Malone in Donnie Darko its eerie afterglow.

lead_characters.name: Denise
lead_characters.hook: David’s younger sister is a small but useful reminder of the family life around him, and her piano detail gives the house a lived-in, generational feel. She helps make David’s world feel rooted and ordinary, which sharpens the film’s magical turn.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a natural child supporting role with a clean, believable beat — the kind of part that gives a young actor a real, specific moment without requiring heavy plot burden.

casting_characteristics: one young female clerk with quiet screen presence

technical.vfx_details: Primarily sound design, shimmer transitions, time-lapse/double-exposure style transitions, and a final unicorn horn transformation that can be achieved with practical makeup plus light digital enhancement.
technical.sfx_needs: Sound-driven magical cues, shimmer effects, and a practical/FX-assisted horn reveal in the final sequence.

rights_flags.detail: If I Got My Ticket, Can I Ride? by The Boys Choir of Harlem

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: specialty theatrical with strong streaming afterlife, or direct-to-streaming for an elevated coming-of-age fantasy audience.

budget.note: Contemporary, mostly practical locations, no action set pieces, and only a light VFX/sound-design lift keep this comfortably in indie territory.

casting.note: The lead requires a very specific mix of guarded naturalism, queer interiority, and final-act emotional release; David also needs genuine sincerity without tipping into preciousness.

development.note: The middle section is intentionally elliptical and mood-led, so the buyer conversation will center on whether the search structure feels cumulative enough before the final transformation lands.

comp_set.title: The Half of It
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the queer coming-of-age intimacy, restrained emotional register, and young-woman POV that turns identity into the real engine.

comp_set.title: Thelma
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the slow-burn supernatural awakening and the way bodily transformation becomes a metaphor for self-recognition.

comp_set.title: A Ghost Story
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on lyrical pacing, visual patience, and the willingness to let atmosphere carry meaning as much as plot.

comp_set.title: After Yang
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the meditative sci-fi/fantasy-adjacent tone, family texture, and emotional restraint around identity and memory.

audience_target.primary_audience: Viewers who respond to intimate queer coming-of-age stories with magical realism and a strong emotional payoff.
audience_target.demographics: Primarily 18-34, skewing female and queer, with strong appeal to festival audiences and prestige-streaming viewers who like elevated genre.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, small cast, and minimal effects keep the film in a contained indie feature range, with the final horn reveal as the main specialty shot.

types_of_buyers: prestige-minded producers looking for a queer breakout
lane_fit.detail: The script sits naturally in the lane where emotional specificity and a distinctive visual language matter more than scale. It’s the kind of project that can be sold on tone, lead performance, and a clean high-concept metaphor rather than on spectacle.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a complete emotional arc; the supporting characters are vivid but not built as spinoff anchors.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The unicorn reveal is identity, not gimmick.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the film a clean emotional engine buyers can understand quickly: the fantasy element is the payoff to an internal coming-of-age story, not decoration. It’s especially attractive to streamers and indie financiers looking for elevated genre with a clear thematic hook.
strengths.evidence: The final mirror sequence, the forehead shimmer, and the horn emerging from Alma’s face turn the magical premise into a self-recognition moment.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Alma is a strong lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The role has contradiction, restraint, and a late emotional bloom, which is exactly the kind of part that can launch or reframe a young actor. Casting directors and talent reps will see a showcase for interiority, dry humor, and a final transformation beat.
strengths.evidence: Her gas-station skepticism, the fight in the woods, and the quiet mirror scene all reveal different registers of the same character.

strengths.what_it_means: That gives the project a directorial signature that can separate it from standard indie coming-of-age fare and make it feel festival-ready. Buyers who respond to formal confidence will see a filmmaker with a point of view, not just a premise.
strengths.evidence: The opening silent birthday, the shimmer cues, the slowed world under the table, and the recurring sonic motif all build a consistent language.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The bilingual family texture feels lived-in.
strengths.what_it_means: That broadens authenticity and gives the film cultural specificity without turning it into issue drama. It helps the project speak to Latino audiences and to buyers looking for a contemporary, rooted voice.
strengths.evidence: The Spanish dialogue with Alma’s mother, the church setting, and the domestic details in both homes create a credible family world.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The final image lands with emotional clarity.
strengths.what_it_means: A clean, memorable ending is a real commercial asset because it gives the film a trailerable payoff and a strong word-of-mouth image. The ending also signals that the movie knows exactly what it is, which helps buyers trust the package.
strengths.evidence: The horn reveal, the embrace, and the return to the childhood field image create a complete visual and emotional button.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, performance-forward indie fantasy with a real festival-and-streaming lane: a queer coming-of-age story that uses unicorn mythology as a clean metaphor for self-recognition. The production footprint stays small while the final transformation gives the movie a memorable image buyers can market around.

items.area: The middle search is mood-first, not engine-first.
items.detail: A long stretch of car rides, woods wandering, and repeated conversation carries the film on atmosphere more than escalation. That’s a real buyer conversation for a feature: the ending pays off, but the central drive is intentionally elliptical rather than propulsive.

items.area: David is vivid, but the film is Alma’s movie.
items.detail: He has the more active quest, yet the emotional and thematic resolution belongs to Alma, which makes the lead/supporting balance feel asymmetrical. That’s not a flaw in the material, but it does mean the packaging conversation will center almost entirely on the actress playing Alma.

items.area: The final horn reveal is a specialty shot.
items.detail: The ending needs the horn to feel both beautiful and unsettling, which means the makeup/VFX execution has to be precise or the payoff softens. It’s still a modest effects ask, but it is the one sequence where craft execution is directly tied to audience belief.

items.area: The music clearances are not incidental.
items.detail: Skyline To by Frank Ocean, If I Got My Ticket, Can I Ride? by The Boys Choir of Harlem, and Anything by Adriene Lanker are all named in the script and shape the film’s emotional texture. That creates real clearance and budget work if the production wants to preserve the exact needle-drop identity.

issues.headline: The script’s main friction is structural rather than conceptual: the premise is clear and the ending is strong, but the central search plays as a long, reflective drift before it becomes a payoff. The other producer conversations will be about protecting the final transformation shot and deciding how much of the named music identity is worth clearing.
